chapters.title: Chapter 2: Yield Measures and What They Really Mean

lessons.title: Solving for YTM: Trial and Error, Approximation, and Excel's YIELD Function

children.text: You now know that yield to maturity is the discount rate that makes a bond's cash flows equal its price. The catch: for any bond with more than two cash flows, there is no formula you can rearrange to isolate it. Bond desks at SBI and HDFC Bank, the NSE's RFQ platform and RBI Retail Direct all compute YTM by the same underlying method: guess, check, and refine. This lesson teaches you three ways to do it, from pencil and paper to a single Excel cell, and when each one can be trusted.

body.text: Finding YTM is a search, not a formula. Every method, from your guesses on paper to Excel's YIELD function, keeps adjusting the discount rate until the bond's present value matches its price.

children.text: An illustrative AAA-rated PSU bond on the NSE RFQ platform: 8.40% coupon paid semi-annually, exactly six years to maturity, priced on a coupon date at ₹103.20 per ₹100 face value. That gives 12 half-year periods, a ₹4.20 coupon each period, and ₹100 at the end. We need the YTM that solves:

body.caption: A 12th-degree equation in YTM. No algebraic rearrangement gives the answer directly.

children.text: Method 1: Trial and Error, Then Interpolate
Start with what you already know. The price is above ₹100, so this is a premium bond and the YTM must be below the 8.40% coupon. Then use one rule to steer every guess:
if your trial price is too high, your guessed yield is too low, so raise it; if your trial price is too low, lower the yield.

body.caption: Searching for the YTM that gives a price of ₹103.20

markDefs.definition: Estimating a value between two known points by assuming a straight line between them.

children.text: Once you have bracketed the answer, you do not need more guesses. Over a narrow 10 basis point range the price curve is almost a straight line, so
gets you extremely close. The target price ₹103.20 is 0.1136 below the 7.70% price, out of a total gap of 0.4817 between the two guesses.

body.caption: y₁, y₂ = the two bracketing yields; P₁, P₂ = their prices; P = market price. The exact YTM is 7.7235%, so interpolation is off by 0.0001%.

body.title: Steer the next guess
body.question: You are solving for the YTM of a bond priced at ₹97.50. At a trial yield of 7.20%, you get a price of ₹98.60. What should your next guess be?
options: A lower yield, such as 7.00%, because the trial price is too high
A higher yield, such as 7.40%, because the trial price is too high
A lower yield, such as 7.00%, because the bond is at a discount
Keep 7.20%, because the prices are within ₹1.10
body.explanation: ₹98.60 is above the ₹97.50 market price, so the discount rate is too low. Raising the yield shrinks every present value and brings the trial price down towards ₹97.50.

children.text: When you need a quick estimate on a phone calculator, say while an RM is pitching you a bond over a call, use the approximation formula. The logic is intuitive: your annual return is roughly the coupon plus the pull-to-par gain (or minus the loss) spread evenly over the years left, divided by the average of what you pay and what you get back.

body.caption: C = annual coupon in ₹, FV = face value, P = price, N = years to maturity. For our bond: (8.40 + (100 − 103.20) ÷ 6) ÷ ((100 + 103.20) ÷ 2) = 7.8667 ÷ 101.60 = 7.74%.

stats.label: Approximation error
stats.context: Good enough for a first check

body.title: Estimate YTM on a phone calculator
body.prompt: An illustrative SDL pays a 7.80% annual coupon (semi-annually), has 8 years left and is quoted at ₹96.40. Use the approximation formula to estimate its YTM. Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Numerator = 7.80 + (100 − 96.40) ÷ 8 = 7.80 + 0.45 = 8.25. Denominator = (100 + 96.40) ÷ 2 = 98.20. Estimate = 8.25 ÷ 98.20 = 8.40%. The exact semi-annual YTM is 8.43%, so the shortcut is about 3 bps low.

body.caption: How accurate is the approximation? (semi-annual bonds unless stated)

body.text: The approximation treats the pull-to-par gain as if it arrived in equal slices every year and ignores compounding. That is harmless for bonds priced near ₹100, but the error balloons for deep discounts and long maturities, as the 20-year bond at ₹70 shows. Never use it to choose between two bonds whose yields are within about 25 bps of each other.

children.text: In practice, you will use a spreadsheet. There are two functions, and which one you use depends on whether you are on a coupon date.

columns.label: RATE (on a coupon date)
points: Returns the yield per period, so multiply by 2 for semi-annual bonds
Only correct when the next coupon is exactly one full period away
No dates, no day count, no accrued interest

columns.label: YIELD (any settlement date)
points: =YIELD(settlement, maturity, coupon rate, clean price, redemption, frequency, basis)
Handles fractional periods and accrued interest internally
Takes the clean price, the one quoted on screen
Basis 4 (30/360) for G-Secs and SDLs, basis 1 (Actual/Actual) for corporate bonds

children.text: Check it against a bond you already know. In Chapter 1, Kavita bought the 7.18% GS 2033 at a clean price of ₹103.73 when it was trading at a 6.50% yield. Run it backwards: =YIELD(DATE(2026,9,15), DATE(2033,8,14), 7.18%, 103.73, 100, 2, 4) returns 6.50%. Price to yield and yield to price are the same equation, solved in opposite directions.

body.title: Pick the function
body.textWithBlank: To calculate the YTM of a G-Sec bought between coupon dates in Excel, using its settlement date, maturity date and quoted clean price, use the ___ function.
body.explanation: YIELD handles the settlement date, fractional first period and accrued interest. RATE works only on a coupon date, when every cash flow is exactly one period apart.

body.title: Show me how a computer searches for YTM (Python)

children.text: The code below does exactly what you did by hand, but systematically. It keeps a low and a high yield that bracket the answer, prices the bond at the midpoint, and halves the bracket each time. After 100 halvings the bracket is far narrower than any market convention needs. Excel's YIELD uses a faster search, but the idea is identical.

content.caption: A bisection search for YTM on a coupon date.

body.title: The RM's "7.8% yield"
body.scenario: Suresh Deshpande, a 58-year-old business owner in Nagpur, gets a call from his private banker offering an illustrative AAA-rated bond: 7.95% annual coupon, ₹10,000 face value, exactly four years to maturity, priced at ₹10,185 on its coupon date. The banker says: "It yields 7.8%, better than the 7.5% you are getting elsewhere." Suresh is considering 490 bonds, about ₹50 lakh.
body.prompt: Work out what the banker's 7.8% really is, estimate the true YTM with the approximation formula, confirm it with Excel, and tell Suresh whether the pitch holds up.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Per ₹100 face value, the price is ₹101.85 and the annual coupon ₹7.95.
2. The banker's 7.8% is the current yield: ₹7.95 ÷ ₹101.85 = 7.81%. It ignores the ₹185 per bond that will be lost when the bond repays ₹10,000 at maturity.
3. Approximation: (7.95 + (100 − 101.85) ÷ 4) ÷ ((100 + 101.85) ÷ 2) = 7.4875 ÷ 100.925 = 7.42%.
4. Exact YTM in Excel: =RATE(4, 7.95, -101.85, 100) returns 7.40%. (On a non-coupon date, he would use YIELD with basis 1.)
5. So the bond yields about 7.40%, below the 7.5% Suresh already earns, not above it. On 490 bonds costing ₹49,90,650, the 40 bp gap between the quoted and true yield is worth roughly ₹20,000 a year.
6. Suresh should ask the banker for the YTM, not the "yield", compare it with recent trades in similar AAA bonds on the NSE or BSE RFQ platforms, and check whether the price includes a distribution spread.

body.title: Before trusting a YIELD result in Excel
steps: Settlement date is the actual settlement date (usually T+1), not the trade date.
Maturity date is the exact redemption date from RBI Retail Direct, CCIL or the issue documents, not just the year.
Coupon rate is entered as a percentage, such as 7.18%, not 7.18.
Price is the clean price per ₹100 face value. For a ₹10,000 or ₹1,000 bond, divide by 100 or 10 first.
Frequency is 2 for G-Secs and SDLs; check the offer document for corporate bonds, many of which pay annually.
Basis is 4 for G-Secs and SDLs, 1 for listed corporate bonds.
Sanity-check the ordering: for a premium bond the YTM must be below the current yield, for a discount bond above it.

points: There is no algebraic formula for YTM. Every method searches for the rate that makes present value equal the price.
Trial and error: if the trial price is too high, raise the yield; too low, lower it. Bracket the answer, then interpolate.
Interpolation over a 10 bp bracket gave 7.7236% against an exact 7.7235%.
The approximation formula, (C + (FV − P) ÷ N) ÷ ((FV + P) ÷ 2), is fine near par but can miss by 40 bps or more on deep discount, long bonds.
Use RATE on coupon dates (multiply by the frequency) and YIELD on any other date, with the clean price and the right basis.
A quoted "yield" is often the current yield. Always ask for, or calculate, the YTM.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Bonds, prices, investors and banker quotes are illustrative. Spreadsheet functions give correct results only with correct inputs; verify coupon dates, day count conventions and settlement dates from RBI Retail Direct, CCIL, NSE, BSE or the issue documents, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
